title: Field trial: directional unit metering with grace credits and streaming multiplier
creator: Priya Kapoor
description:
Objective: run a controlled field trial to evaluate asymmetric per-unit metering (separate ingress vs egress unit rates) combined with a streaming-response multiplier and a customer-level grace credit bucket. We want to validate whether directional pricing plus a small monthly grace allowance increases revenue predictability without materially reducing platform adoption or developer experience.

Hypotheses:
1) Charging a higher rate for egress (output tokens) relative to ingress will better align cost-to-serve with customer value for multi-turn chat workloads and increase ASP for heavy-output use cases.
2) A modest streaming multiplier (a multiplier applied to streamed responses to account for connection overhead) will nudge users toward batched / non-streamed calls where cost sensitivity is highest while preserving streaming for latency-critical paths.
3) Providing a small monthly grace bucket (e.g., first N IO-equivalent units free or heavily discounted) will smooth adoption friction and reduce churn for low-volume/proof-of-concept customers.

Experiment design summary:
- Treatment variants: control (status quo unified per-token price) vs Variant A (egress 1.4x ingress) vs Variant B (egress 1.4x + streaming multiplier 1.2x) vs Variant C (Variant B + monthly grace 5k-unit credit).
- Target population: new signups over 8-week window + a matched holdout of 10% of mid-tier existing accounts (opt-in via sales for enterprise pilots).
- Measurement window: 8 weeks exposure, 8 weeks post-exposure follow-up for churn and adoption metrics.
- Primary success metrics: net revenue per active account (NRPAA), conversion rate from free->paid, trial-to-first-commit, API latency percentiles unaffected, streaming usage retention. Secondary: developer satisfaction via in-product survey, increased requests to sales for contract changes.

Modeling assumptions & cost inputs:
- Runtime cost model assumes average token generation cost of $0.000018 per output token at baseline hardware and $0.000009 per input token served (pre-quantization). We added network egress amortized cost for streaming sessions which motivated the streaming multiplier.
- Sensitivity buckets for workloads: short-turn (<=200 tokens), medium (200-2k), long (>2k).
- Customer-facing price ladder will be tested at small deltas to limit large behavioral shocks.

Operational requirements & dependencies:
- Billing team: support for directional metering (ingress vs egress counters) and streaming multiplier flag in billing pipeline (ENG-4123).
- Console/UI: display directional usage breakdown on per-route and per-token dashboards and add grace-credit visibility (ENG-4891).
- Runtime: tag streamed responses for multiplier attribution and expose a stable event to ingestion pipeline (ENG-4290).
- Legal & Sales: review of enterprise contract language to reflect directional metering and grace credits (Legal PRD: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/LEGAL/Directional+Pricing+Contract+Templates).

Rollout & guardrails:
- Start with 5% of new signups for Variant A, incrementally add Variants B and C after billing and runtime validation.
- Soft cap: automatically revert accounts whose monthly bill increases >50% without a proportional usage increase in value metrics.
- Monitor spikes in support tickets and/or complaints from SDKs (within 24h of assignment to new variant).

Risks and trade-offs:
- Complexity for customers: directional metering increases invoice complexity and may increase support load. Grace credits mitigate initial friction but add accounting overhead.
- Revenue unpredictability: while per-unit deltas aim to improve unit economics, behavioral changes (e.g., batching) could lower per-token revenue.
- Enterprise procurement friction: contracts and security questionnaires must be updated to explain new metering to procurement teams.

Success criteria (go/no-go):
- Go: Variant C yields >=10% uplift in NRPAA among mid-size customers and <3% drop in new-signup-to-paid conversion; developer satisfaction score >= baseline - 5 points.
- No-go: Significant negative impact on developer experience (NPS drop >10 points), >5% uplift in inbound enterprise objections requiring contract amendment, or billing integrity incidents.
